journal.outbreak.common_cold.what: A mild infection of the nose and throat caused by many different viruses. Common signs are a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, a sore throat and a cough. Most people feel better within a week to ten days.
journal.outbreak.common_cold.spread: The viruses travel in tiny droplets that leave the nose and mouth when someone coughs or sneezes. They can also move from hands or objects to someone's face.
journal.outbreak.common_cold.helps: Rest, plenty of fluids and simple remedies that ease the symptoms. Antibiotics do not work against viruses. Anyone with trouble breathing, a very high fever or symptoms that keep getting worse should see a doctor.
journal.outbreak.common_cold.prevent: Wash hands often, cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow, keep unwashed hands away from your face, and stay home when you are unwell.
journal.outbreak.common_cold.game: Villagers sneeze and cough. It spreads between villagers who stand close together, and left alone it fades slowly. A Supportive Tonic speeds up recovery.
journal.outbreak.common_cold.sources: Based on general public health guidance from the CDC and the NHS, put into our own words. Their websites have the full, current advice.
journal.outbreak.seasonal_allergies.what: An overreaction of the body's defences to something harmless, such as pollen. It is not an infection. Typical signs are sneezing, a runny or itchy nose, and itchy, watery eyes, often at the same time every year.
journal.outbreak.seasonal_allergies.spre: It does not pass from person to person. It is set off by triggers such as pollen, dust or animal dander in the air or on surfaces, not by catching it from someone else.
journal.outbreak.seasonal_allergies.help: Staying away from known triggers helps when possible. Antihistamine medicines can ease the symptoms, and a pharmacist or doctor can suggest what suits a person. Wheezing, chest tightness, or a swollen face or throat needs urgent medical help.
journal.outbreak.seasonal_allergies.prev: People check pollen forecasts, keep windows closed on high-pollen days, and wash or change clothes after being outdoors to remove pollen.
journal.outbreak.seasonal_allergies.game: Villagers sneeze now and then. It never spreads between villagers, and it does not go away by itself. An Antihistamine eases it.
journal.outbreak.seasonal_allergies.sour: Based on general public health guidance from the CDC and the NHS, put into our own words. Their websites have the full, current advice.
journal.outbreak.influenza.what: A contagious illness of the nose, throat and lungs caused by influenza viruses. It often starts suddenly with fever, chills, aching muscles, a dry cough and tiredness, and usually feels worse than a cold. Most people recover in a week or two, but it can be serious for older adults, young children, pregnant people and people with long-term health conditions.
journal.outbreak.influenza.spread: Mainly through droplets from coughs and sneezes. A person can pass it on a day or so before they feel ill, and for several days afterwards.
journal.outbreak.influenza.helps: Rest, fluids and staying home. Doctors sometimes prescribe antiviral medicines, especially for people at higher risk. Get medical help for trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, or a fever that will not go away.
journal.outbreak.influenza.prevent: A yearly flu vaccine, washing hands, covering coughs and sneezes, staying home when ill, and bringing fresh air into crowded rooms.
journal.outbreak.influenza.game: Villagers cough, shiver and sneeze. It spreads further than a cold, and a villager can pass it on before looking ill. Left alone it can linger for a very long time. A Supportive Tonic helps.
journal.outbreak.influenza.sources: Based on general public health guidance from the CDC, the WHO and the NHS, put into our own words. Their websites have the full, current advice.
journal.outbreak.food_poisoning.what: Illness caused by eating or drinking something contaminated with germs such as bacteria, viruses or parasites, or with the toxins they make. Common signs are nausea, vomiting, stomach cramps and diarrhoea, sometimes with a fever. Many people get better within a few days.
journal.outbreak.food_poisoning.spread: Mostly through contaminated food or water, or food handled with unwashed hands or dirty tools. Some of the germs can also pass from person to person on hands and surfaces.
journal.outbreak.food_poisoning.helps: Rest and small, frequent sips of fluid to replace what is lost; oral rehydration drinks are made for this. Get medical help for blood in vomit or stools, a high fever, signs of dehydration such as dizziness or very dark urine, or if it lasts more than a few days. Babies, older adults and pregnant people should get advice early.
journal.outbreak.food_poisoning.prevent: Wash hands before cooking and eating, keep raw and cooked foods apart, cook food thoroughly, chill leftovers promptly, wash fruit and vegetables, and use safe water.
journal.outbreak.food_poisoning.game: Villagers clutch their stomachs and shiver. It only spreads between villagers who stand close together and carry food. Oral Rehydration Salts help.
journal.outbreak.food_poisoning.sources: Based on general public health guidance from the WHO, the CDC and the NHS, put into our own words. Their websites have the full, current advice.
journal.outbreak.tools.1: Watch the villagers. Head shakes, coughs, sneezes and small particles can mean a villager is ill, but many illnesses look alike.
journal.outbreak.tools.2: Examination Tool: use it on a villager to see which symptoms they have shown lately and how often. It shows what you can see, never what the illness is.
journal.outbreak.tools.3: Sterile Swab: use it on a villager while you carry an Empty Petri Dish to make a Prepared Petri Dish. Samples go stale after three days.
journal.outbreak.tools.4: Microscope: place the dish on the stage, open it, adjust the focus until the image is sharp, and examine at each magnification. Doctors look at which immune cells and particles are present: viral infections tend to raise lymphocytes, allergies tend to raise eosinophils, and bacterial infections tend to raise neutrophils. Gather enough evidence, then choose a diagnosis.
journal.outbreak.tools.5: Treatment: use a treatment item on a villager who shows symptoms. If it is the wrong item, nothing is wasted and the item is kept.
journal.outbreak.tools.6: This journal records your own diagnoses. Other players cannot see them.
journal.outbreak.about.1: Outbreak is a simplified game. The illnesses, symptoms, timings and treatments are invented to be playable and do not match real medicine.
journal.outbreak.about.2: Nothing in this mod is medical advice, a diagnosis or a treatment. If you or someone you know feels unwell, talk to a doctor, pharmacist or local health service. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.
journal.outbreak.about.3: The background pages use general public health guidance from the CDC, the WHO and the NHS, put into our own words. Their websites have complete, up-to-date information.
